terms.grammar: enclitic, on the first word of the question, with the subjunctive
evidence: Cato Agr. 2.1: satisne temperī opera sient cōnfecta, possitne quae reliqua sient cōnficere
terms.comment: An indirect question is a direct one put under a verb of asking, knowing or telling: the -ne stays and the verb goes into the subjunctive.

evidence: Cic. Off. 3.59: quaerit ex proximō vīcīnō, num fēriae quaedam piscātōrum essent
terms.comment: In an indirect question the same as -ne, without the “surely not” of a direct num.

terms.grammar: conjunction, after verbs of trying, waiting and looking
evidence: Petr. 33.2: temptēmus tamen, sī adhūc sorbilia sunt
Phaedr. 4.8.3–4: haec cum temptāret sī qua rēs esset cibī
terms.comment: “To see whether”, after temptāre, experīrī, exspectāre, vidēre (Lewis & Short s.v. si).

terms.grammar: conjunction, after verbs of doubting and not knowing
evidence: Plin. Ep. 2.2.1: nec liquet mihi an dēbeam
terms.comment: After dubitō, nesciō, haud sciō it leans towards yes: haud sciō an, I rather think.

phrases.latin: vīlicum vocet, roget quid operis siet factum, quid restet, satisne temperī opera sient cōnfecta, possitne quae reliqua sient cōnficere
phrases.english: let him call the overseer and ask what work has been done, what is left, whether the jobs were finished in time, whether he can finish what remains

phrases.latin: quaerit ex proximō vīcīnō, num fēriae quaedam piscātōrum essent, quod eōs nūllōs vidēret
phrases.english: he asks the nearest neighbour whether it was some fishermen’s holiday, since he saw none of them

phrases.latin: timeō nē jam conceptī sint. temptēmus tamen, sī adhūc sorbilia sunt
phrases.english: I’m afraid they have chicks in them already. Let’s try, though, whether they can still be sucked

phrases.latin: īrāscor, nec liquet mihi an dēbeam, sed īrāscor
phrases.english: I am angry, and I am not sure whether I ought to be, but I am angry

sources: Lewis & Short: ne · Lewis & Short: num · Lewis & Short: si · Lewis & Short: an
